title: The confidence men Big and Little Harry, and how they protected her
summary: Harry Merrill and Little Harry conned people, once her stepfather out of his grocery, but taught her how not to be turned into a bad girl.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: So then they had Harry Merrill. They called him Big Harry. He was a confidence man. And Little Harry was a confidence man. They were -- wouldn't exactly call them pimps because they made their own money by confidencing people, you see. In fact they confidenced my stepfather out of his grocery, out of his grocery store. Yes, they did. I didn't know it was them until years after. And I found it was Harry, Big Harry and Little Harry, confidenced my stepfather.
Did they know he was your stepfather?

No, they didn't know it was my stepfather. They wouldn't have done it. You know, those fellows had honor, as it went, you know, as their honor went, they had honor. But anyhow, there was Lumsie, Big Harry, Little Harry, and there was another fellow there, a fellow named Montgomery. Can't think of his first name. Sam Montgomery. Now, he was a pimp. So every night they would come up and the girls would check in to see which one brought in the most money, and Tacky Annie always came first. And incidentally, Tacky Annie started going with Mr. Hoskins who owned the little club, Hugh Hoskins. He had a wife upstairs and a little boy, but the wife, you know, she was one of those real housewives that didn't know that it was raining when it was. And so she would cash in. Tacky Annie would come in with a handful of
wallets, where she'd stolen money from everybody.
She was not a prostitute. She --
She wasn't a prostitute. She was a pickpocket.
And the pickpockets had pimps, too?
Huh? Yes. Most all the pickpockets had pimps.

All the pickpockets had pimps. But Harry Merrill and Little Harry and them, they were the confidence men. They made their own money by confidencing people out of their own money, you see. But I'll tell you how nice they were. They saw that I was a young person, naive, and didn't know whether it was raining, so they taught me how not to let anybody make a bad girl out of me.

Wasn't that wonderful? They taught me how not to let -- they showed me how. The fellows would take an innocent girl, a girl that didn't know, you know, exactly right from wrong in that particular field, and they would take her downtown and dress her up in beautiful clothes and everything, and show her what she could have if she'd just live the wrong life. You understand?
